paragraphs.text: A cake of [Liu Bao](liu-bao:definition) from 1999, made under [Three Cranes](three-cranes:definition), the trademark of Wuzhou Tea Factory, the largest maker of this [dark tea](dark:definition). The mark belongs to that one factory and names neither a grade of leaf nor a village. Around 1958 the same factory worked out [cold-water piling](liu-bao:making-factory): the leaf is wetted, heaped at a modest warmth and turned until it darkens, a steadier route than the farmhouse steaming that came before.

The city stands in the east of Guangxi on the Guangdong border, where the Xi and Gui rivers meet. The tea takes its name from Liubao town in [Cangwu County](guangxi:wuzhou-and-cangwu), in the countryside under the city. The city itself was where leaf from the hills was gathered, finished and sent downriver on what the trade still calls the [old tea boat road](wuzhou:liu-bao-trade), to Guangzhou and then by sea to the Chinese workers of Southeast Asia.

At twenty-seven years this cake is well past the ten after which the trade counts a Liu Bao as [aged](liu-bao:age-aged). How it was stored matters as much as how long, and the trade does not agree whether such tea keeps improving for decades or peaks sooner.

brewing.text: From a brick, cake or basket, ease the leaf off along the edge or from the top with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole pieces give up their flavour steadily; crumbs release it all at once and cloud the cup. Liu Bao takes very hot or boiling water, because its leaf is dense and gives up its depth slowly. Rinse it once or twice and pour the rinse away. Use about 5 to 8 grams to 100 ml, start with steeps of five to fifteen seconds and add a few seconds each round; a good Liu Bao gives ten cups or more.

notice.text: A deep red, thick cup with woody, herbal and betel nut notes; tea several decades old is often described with ginseng and camphor.
